problem: Semi-parametric topological-memory navigation methods (SPTM, ViNG) rely on a graph over all training images, which needs hand-tuned pruning/sparsification to avoid spurious edges, limit memory, and keep queries fast; end-to-end policies (GC-BC) fail on long horizons.
motivation: Graph memory grows with environment size and spurious edges break global planning, while pruning heuristics need per-environment tuning. The authors want a fixed-size, graph-free memory learned from non-expert RGB+action exploration data without pose or depth.
key_idea: Train a temporary graph from self-supervised embeddings to supervise a geodesic regressor, then discard the graph and navigate by greedily minimizing a neural potential (geodesic attractor plus latent repulsors from visited states) over image embeddings.
insight: The geodesic regressor encodes graph geometry in network weights, replacing the graph at test time, and its latent space recovers environment topology without pose (Fig. globals_graphs). Ablations show both potential terms are essential: without the repulsors SR on Easy drops from 0.95 to 0.11 (agent thrashes in local minima), and without the geodesic attractor SR drops to 0.45 on Easy and 0.04 on Very-Hard.
method: Local backbone h: ResNet-18 on front+rear 96x96 RGB with 1D-conv fusion, trained with a temporal contrastive (Siamese) loss with positive margin 1 and negative margin 10, giving a local metric d_h.
Inverse kinematics head: predicts the action between two embeddings or NOT_CONNECTED (cross-entropy, using random negatives), discovering loop closures.
Graph construction: chain graph of observed transitions plus loop-closure edges predicted by the IK head, weighted by d_h, with no pruning; used only during training.
Forward kinematics head: predicts the next embedding from embedding+action, co-trained on graph edges labelled by the IK head.
Geodesic regressor: MLP regressing Dijkstra shortest-path length between embedding pairs (manifold learning objective); one per environment, while h, IK and FK are shared.

Potential-field navigation: pick the collision-free action (laser box check on FORWARD) minimizing G(FK(z,a), z_g) plus sum of repulsors max(0, m_r - d_h) over a buffer of 500 visited embeddings; STOP when d_h to the goal is below a threshold.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 backbone + MLP heads (IK, FK, geodesic regressor), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: 240,000 RGB+action samples from random-waypoint exploration across 8 Gibson scenes in simulation (70/30 train/val); 21,000 teleoperated real-world samples for finetuning
setting.observation: front and back monocular RGB 96x96 (90° FOV each) plus a front laser scan for collision checking only
setting.action_space: discrete: FORWARD 0.25 m, ROTATE_LEFT/RIGHT 15°, STOP (STOP decided by a local-metric threshold)
setting.simulator: Habitat with Gibson; real Jackal UGV
setting.privileged: none at test time (laser scan for collision checking only); oracle stopping only for the Random and GC-BC baselines

numbers.eval_set_note: 8 Gibson environments, 1,000 trajectories per difficulty per environment as described; Easy 1.5-3m
numbers.extra: trained per-environment on the same 8 scenes it is evaluated in; different start/goal positions from data collection; max 500 steps; success radius 1m
numbers.evidence: Table 1, average navigation performance over 8 simulated Gibson environments, Easy column (CFT is averaged across all difficulties)

numbers.eval_set_note: 27 runs (9 episodes x 3 repeats) in a 4.65m x 9.1m lab
numbers.backbone: ResNet-18 + MLP heads finetuned on 21k real samples
numbers.extra: finetuned 30k steps from the simulation checkpoint; |B|=300, thresh=5; max 300 steps
numbers.evidence: Table 2, average Jackal navigation performance over 27 episodes

numbers_note: Simulation metrics are printed as fractions (0-1) in the paper and are copied as printed. The simulation benchmark is a custom Gibson image-goal setup on 8 scenes, not a standard benchmark.
results: O4A reaches SR 0.95/0.93/0.90/0.85 from Easy to Very-Hard with a constant SPL of 0.65. This far exceeds the best baselines (ViNG SR 0.29/0.19/0.11/0.06; SPTM; GC-BC; Random SR 0.49 on Easy). On a real Jackal it achieves SR 0.74 and DTG 0.83 m versus human teleoperation at SR 0.96.
limitations: Still needs one geodesic regressor per environment (and a training graph), so it does not generalize to new scenes without training.
Greedy action selection with 15° discrete turns causes thrashing and many rotation steps in the real world (53 vs 18 for the human).
Does not handle dynamic or semi-static objects; evaluation is on only 8 small Gibson scenes and a single lab.
